[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This playbook walks product owners through the complete journey from "I have a system to specify" to "the engineering team has executable user stories in their sprint backlog." Every project begins with a validated conceptual architecture — if one exists, you validate it; if it does not, you build it. This is not optional. A conceptual architecture is the required input to BDD specification. Once you have one, the playbook guides you through Gherkin scenario authoring, Azure DevOps User Story creation, engineering handoff, and acceptance.
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#who-this-is-for]

### Who This Is For

**Primary:** Product owners, business analysts, and program managers who define what the system should do — regardless of prior BDD experience.

**Secondary:** Engineering leads who want to understand what the product owner is producing and how to consume it.
page_texts.6:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#what-you-will-learn]

### What You Will Learn

By the end of this playbook, you will be able to:

- Establish or validate a conceptual architecture that meets BDD readiness criteria
- Use AI to decompose business requirements into well-formed Gherkin scenarios
- Create Azure DevOps User Stories with Gherkin acceptance criteria at the right level of granularity
- Hand off to engineering with confidence that the spec is unambiguous, testable, and executable
- Know when your job is done and when to re-engage

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#what-you-do-not-need-to-know]

### What You Do Not Need to Know

- You do not need to know any programming language
- You do not need to understand how the CI pipeline works
- You do not need to write step definitions or production code
- You do not need to know what a "step definition" is — that is the engineer's responsibility

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#the-problem-this-solves]

### The Problem This Solves

You write acceptance criteria. An engineer reads them. They build something. Weeks later, at demo or QA, you discover the engineer interpreted your words differently than you intended. The feature is technically complete but behaviorally wrong.

This happens because prose acceptance criteria require translation — from your words to the engineer's mental model to code to tests. Every translation introduces drift.

**BDD eliminates the translation.** You write the acceptance criteria in a structured format (Gherkin) that is simultaneously:

- Readable by you (it is plain English with a Given/When/Then structure)
- Executable by the CI pipeline (it becomes an automated test)
- Unambiguous for the engineer (there is one correct interpretation)

The scenario you write is the test the system must pass. There is no intermediate step where intent can be lost.

## Phase 1: Establish the Conceptual Architecture

A validated conceptual architecture is the required input to BDD specification. You cannot skip this phase. If an architecture exists, you validate it. If it does not, you build it. If it is incomplete, you fill the gaps. Either way, you exit this phase with a document that meets the [BDD readiness checklist (GUID-APP-IMPL-007)](../../application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-007-conceptual-architecture-bdd-readiness-guidance.md).

> **For regulated domains:** If the system operates under regulatory mandates (CFR, state plans), involves legacy modernization, or has enterprise standards that impose obligations, requirements derivation should be performed BEFORE entering this playbook's Phase 3. See [GUID-GOV-PROC-011 — Requirements Engineering for Regulated Domains](./GUID-GOV-PROC-011-requirements-engineering-regulated-domains.md). Derivation produces pre-discovered Rules that accelerate Example Mapping in Step 4.5.
page_texts.12:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#step-1-check-for-an-existing-conceptual-architecture]

### Step 1: Check for an Existing Conceptual Architecture

Look in the project's `docs/design/conceptual/` directory.

| What You Find | What You Do |
|--------------|-------------|
| A conceptual architecture document exists | Read it and proceed to the readiness assessment below |
| Multiple documents exist (one per domain) | Read each one — each domain will have its own concern directories |
| The directory is empty or contains only a README | No architecture exists — proceed to Step 2 to build one |
| A document exists but you are not sure if it is a conceptual architecture | Check whether it contains bounded contexts, capability lists, and a glossary — if yes, assess readiness; if no, proceed to Step 2 |

**Readiness assessment:** If a document exists, check it against the six required elements from [GUID-APP-IMPL-007](../../application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-007-conceptual-architecture-bdd-readiness-guidance.md):

| Required Element | Present? | If Missing |
|-----------------|----------|------------|
| System purpose statement | ☐ | Write one in Step 2 |
| Bounded context map | ☐ | Discover contexts in Step 2 |
| Domain capability inventory | ☐ | Discover capabilities in Step 2 |
| Context relationships | ☐ | Map relationships in Step 2 |
| Domain glossary | ☐ | Build glossary in Step 2 |
| Concern abbreviation table | ☐ | Create abbreviations in Step 2 |

**If all six are present:** Skip to [Step 3](#step-3-validate-bdd-readiness) for final validation.

**If any are missing:** Proceed to Step 2 and complete only the missing elements — you do not need to redo work that already exists.

This step produces the six required elements. If you have an existing document with gaps, work only on the missing elements. If you are starting from scratch, work through all six.
page_texts.14:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#2a-system-purpose-statement]

#### 2a: System Purpose Statement

State what the system does, who it serves, and why it exists. Two to four sentences.

> "I'm specifying a system that [one-sentence job description]. The users are [roles]. It integrates with [external systems]. Help me write a two-sentence purpose statement."

**Output format:**

```markdown
## System Purpose

[System Name] is a [type of system] that [what it does] for [who it serves].
It [business problem it solves], enabling [business outcome].
```

**Validation:** Can you answer "What does this system do?" in one sentence after reading it? If not, it is too vague or too long.
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#2b-bounded-contexts]

#### 2b: Bounded Contexts

Identify the 3–10 major functional areas of the system. These are the bounded contexts — cohesive domains that own their own rules, data, and vocabulary.

**Using AI:**

> "I'm specifying a system that [purpose statement]. Help me identify the major functional areas this system needs. Name them using business language, not technical terms."

AI will suggest groupings. Your job is to validate that the groupings match how the business thinks about the system — not how engineers might organize the code.

**Output:** A bounded context table:

| Bounded Context | Responsibility | Concern Directory |
|-----------------|---------------|-------------------|
| Enrollment | Manages member enrollment applications and status transitions | `enrollment/` |
| Eligibility | Determines member eligibility based on federal and state rules | `eligibility/` |

**Rules:**
- Name contexts using domain language, not technical names (`Enrollment`, not `EnrollmentService`)
- Each context gets a one-sentence responsibility statement
- Map each context to the concern directory name it will use in `docs/requirements/functional/`
- 3–10 contexts — fewer than 3 means the system is too small for BDD decomposition; more than 10 means some contexts need consolidation
page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#2c-domain-capability-inventory]

#### 2c: Domain Capability Inventory

For each bounded context, list the specific things it does — stated as verbs, not nouns. Each capability will become a `.feature` file.

**Using AI:**

> "For the [bounded context] area, what specific capabilities does the system need? List them as actions the system performs, not components or modules."

**Your validation:** For each capability AI suggests, ask yourself: "Would a business stakeholder recognize this as something the system does?" If the answer is "only an engineer would know what that means," the capability is too technical — ask AI to rephrase it in business terms.

**Output:** A capability table for each context:

| Capability | Description | Feature File |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|
| Submit enrollment application | A member submits a new enrollment application with demographic and eligibility information | `submit-enrollment.feature` |
| Review enrollment application | A caseworker reviews a submitted application for completeness and accuracy | `review-enrollment.feature` |

**Rules:**
- State capabilities as verbs: "Submit enrollment application", not "Enrollment submission"
- One-sentence description explaining who does it and what happens
- Map each capability to a `.feature` filename (kebab-case)
- 3–8 capabilities per context — fewer means the context is too narrow; more means split it
- Only domain capabilities visible to a user or actor — not technical operations
page_texts.17:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#2d-context-relationships]

#### 2d: Context Relationships

Describe how bounded contexts interact — what triggers cross-context behavior, what data flows, and the directionality.

**Using AI:**

> "Given these bounded contexts: [list]. What triggers interaction between them? For each relationship, what is the domain event that causes one context to notify or invoke another?"

**Output:**

| Source Context | Target Context | Trigger | Description |
|---------------|---------------|---------|-------------|
| Enrollment | Eligibility | Enrollment submitted | When a new enrollment is submitted, the Eligibility context evaluates the member's eligibility |
| Eligibility | Benefits | Eligibility determined | When a member is determined eligible, the Benefits context assigns the appropriate benefit package |

**Rules:**
- State the trigger as a domain event, not a technical mechanism ("Enrollment submitted", not "Kafka message published")
- Each relationship produces at least one integration scenario in the source context's `.feature` file
- If two contexts have a bidirectional relationship, list both directions
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#2e-domain-glossary]

#### 2e: Domain Glossary

List every domain term used in the bounded contexts, capabilities, and relationships — with precise definitions.

**Using AI:**

> "From the bounded contexts and capabilities I've defined, extract every domain-specific term. Define each one in one sentence. Flag any term that is used with different meanings in different contexts."

**Output:** Add terms to `docs/glossary.md` (cross-cutting) or `docs/design/conceptual/domains/<domain>/glossary.md` (context-specific):

| Term | Definition | Owning Context |
|------|-----------|----------------|
| Enrollment Application | A formal request by a member to enroll in a Medicaid program | Enrollment |
| Eligibility Determination | The process of evaluating an application against federal and state rules | Eligibility |

**Rules:**
- Every noun and verb used in bounded context names, capability descriptions, or relationship triggers must appear in the glossary
- Use the glossary term exactly — no abbreviations, no synonyms
- If a term crosses multiple contexts, it goes in the project-wide glossary with no owning context
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#2f-concern-abbreviation-table]

#### 2f: Concern Abbreviation Table

Create a 2–4 character abbreviation for each bounded context, used in `@FR-` requirement tags.

**Using AI:**

> "I have these bounded contexts: [list]. Suggest a 2–4 character uppercase abbreviation for each. The abbreviation will be used in requirement tags like @FR-ENR-SUB-010."

**Your validation:**
- Each abbreviation is unique within the project — check `docs/requirements/functional/README.md` for existing abbreviations
- Each abbreviation is recognizable without looking it up
- Once published, abbreviations must not change (they are embedded in `@FR-` tags)

**Output:** A concern abbreviation table ready to be added to the project's `docs/requirements/functional/README.md`. Share this with the engineering lead — they will create the directory structure.
page_texts.20:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#step-3-validate-bdd-readiness]

### Step 3: Validate BDD Readiness

Before proceeding to Gherkin authoring, validate the conceptual architecture against the [GUID-APP-IMPL-007 BDD Readiness Checklist](../../application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-007-conceptual-architecture-bdd-readiness-guidance.md#bdd-readiness-checklist):

**Required Elements:**

- [ ] System purpose statement — 2–4 sentences answering what, who, and why
- [ ] Bounded context map — 3–10 named contexts, each with a responsibility statement and concern directory mapping
- [ ] Domain capability inventory — 3–8 capabilities per context, stated as verbs, each mapped to a `.feature` filename
- [ ] Context relationships — triggers, directionality, and which `.feature` files need integration scenarios
- [ ] Domain glossary — all terms defined, each assigned to an owning context
- [ ] Concern abbreviation table — 2–4 character abbreviations, unique within the project

**Quality Checks:**

- [ ] All bounded context names use domain language, not technical names
- [ ] All capabilities are verbs, not nouns or technical operations
- [ ] All glossary terms are used consistently throughout the document
- [ ] No abbreviation collides with an existing concern in the project
- [ ] The document contains no implementation details

**Gate:** Do not proceed to Phase 2 until all required elements are present and quality checks pass. If any element is missing, return to the relevant sub-step in Step 2.

> **You now have a validated conceptual architecture.** This document — whether you built it from scratch or received it from an architect — is the foundation for all BDD specification work that follows.

## Phase 2: Select Capabilities for This Sprint
page_texts.22:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#step-4-choose-what-to-specify-now]

### Step 4: Choose What to Specify Now

You do not specify the entire system at once. Select the capabilities from your conceptual architecture that are planned for the current sprint or iteration.

**Selection criteria:**

| Question | If Yes |
|----------|--------|
| Is this capability in the sprint backlog? | Specify it now |
| Does this capability have unresolved business rules? | Resolve the rules first, then specify |
| Does this capability depend on another that has not been built yet? | Specify it, but note the dependency — the engineer handles ordering |
| Is this capability well-understood by the team? | Good candidate for specification |
| Is this capability still being debated by stakeholders? | Do not specify yet — stabilize the requirement first |

**Output:** A short list of capabilities (typically 1–5 per sprint) that you will decompose into Gherkin scenarios in Phase 3.

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#step-45-example-mapping--discover-rules-before-writing-gherkin]

### Step 4.5: Example Mapping — Discover Rules Before Writing Gherkin

Before drafting scenarios, use Example Mapping to decompose the capability into testable business rules:

**What is Example Mapping?**

A structured discovery technique (Matt Wynne, 2015) that produces three outputs from a business capability:

| Output | What It Is | What It Becomes |
|--------|-----------|-----------------|
| **Rules** | Named business rules that govern behavior | `Rule:` keyword entries in the `.feature` file |
| **Examples** | Concrete instances of each rule (happy path, edge, error) | Gherkin Scenarios under each Rule |
| **Questions** | Unknowns that need answers before proceeding | Items to resolve with stakeholders before authoring |

**How to run an Example Mapping session:**

1. State the capability being specified (from the conceptual architecture)
2. Ask: "What are the rules that govern this capability?" — list each as a one-sentence business rule
3. For each rule, ask: "Give me a concrete example of this rule in action" — describe a specific case with real values
4. For each rule, ask: "What's an edge case?" and "What happens when this rule is violated?"
5. Note anything uncertain as a Question — these must be resolved before Gherkin can be written

**If derivation decisions exist** (from `/eap-disc-requirements-derive` + `/eap-disc-requirements-synthesize`):
- The INCLUDE decisions are pre-discovered Rules — present them and ask the PO to validate
- The PO adds any missing Rules, removes irrelevant ones, and answers remaining Questions

**If no derivation exists:**
- Discover Rules interactively with the PO using the questions above
- AI assists by suggesting edge cases and error conditions the PO may not have considered

**Output of Example Mapping:**
- A list of 3–8 Rules (named business rules)
- 1–3 Examples per Rule (will become scenarios)
- 0–N Questions (must be resolved before proceeding to Step 5)

**Gate:** Do not proceed to Step 5 (Gherkin drafting) while Questions remain unresolved. Resolve them with the relevant stakeholder first.
page_texts.25:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#step-5-draft-scenarios-with-ai]

### Step 5: Draft Scenarios with AI

For each capability you selected, work with AI to draft the Gherkin scenarios.

**The conversation:**

Start by telling AI what you are specifying:

> "I need to write BDD Gherkin scenarios for the [capability] capability in the [concern] area. The system should [plain language description of what the system does]. The users are [roles]. Here are the business rules: [list any rules, constraints, or edge cases you know about]."

AI will generate draft scenarios. Then guide it:

> "What edge cases am I missing? What happens when [input] is invalid? What happens when [external system] is unavailable? What about [boundary condition]?"

**What AI produces:**

```gherkin
@enrollment
Feature: Enrollment submission validation
  All enrollment submissions are validated before processing. Invalid
  submissions return specific error codes identifying the failing field.

  @FR-ENR-SUB-010
  Scenario: Complete enrollment submission is accepted
    Given a member submits an enrollment with all required fields
    When the submission is validated
    Then the validation result is "accepted"

  @FR-ENR-SUB-020
  Scenario: Missing email address is rejected
    Given a member submits an enrollment without an email address
    When the submission is validated
    Then the validation result is "rejected"
    And the error code is "EMAIL_REQUIRED"
```

**What you must check (AI cannot do this for you):**

| Check | Why |
|-------|-----|
| Do the scenarios match the actual business requirement? | AI can structure; only you know what the business actually needs |
| Are the concrete values correct? | AI may guess at error codes, threshold values, or business rules — verify them against the source of truth |
| Are the edge cases real? | AI may suggest edge cases that cannot occur in your domain — remove them |
| Is anything missing? | AI may not know about regulatory constraints, compliance rules, or business decisions that have not been documented |
page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#step-6-validate-and-refine-the-scenarios]

### Step 6: Validate and Refine the Scenarios

Before the scenarios leave your hands, apply this checklist:

- [ ] **Every scenario answers one question:** "What does the system do when [specific condition]?"
- [ ] **Concrete values everywhere:** No "valid input" or "correct result" — use actual values like `"America/New_York"` or `"EMAIL_REQUIRED"`
- [ ] **Domain vocabulary only:** Every noun and verb matches `docs/glossary.md` — if a term is not in the glossary, add it or ask the architect
- [ ] **No implementation details:** Steps say _what_ happens, never _how_ — "the submission is validated" not "the ValidationService.Validate method is called"
- [ ] **One When per scenario:** If you wrote two `When` steps, you are testing two behaviors — split into two scenarios
- [ ] **No real data:** All example values are synthetic — no real names, emails, member IDs, or dates from production
- [ ] **Happy path + error paths:** At minimum, one scenario for the expected behavior and one for each known error condition
- [ ] **3–15 scenarios per file:** Fewer than 3 means the capability is too narrow; more than 15 means it should be split

For the full syntax reference (tagging format, Scenario Outlines, step keywords), consult [GUID-APP-IMPL-006](../../application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md).

**Output:** A draft `.feature` file ready for engineering review.

## Phase 4: Create Azure DevOps User Stories
page_texts.28:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#step-7-create-the-user-story]

### Step 7: Create the User Story

Each `.feature` file becomes one Azure DevOps User Story. Use AI to generate the story from your scenarios:

> "Create an Azure DevOps User Story from this `.feature` file. Use this format: Title is [Concern] — [Capability summary]. Story is As a / I need / So that. Acceptance criteria are the Gherkin scenarios verbatim — do not summarize or paraphrase them."

**The story structure:**

```
Title:   [Concern] — [Capability summary]
         Example: Enrollment — Submission validation

Story:   As a member
         I need my enrollment submission validated immediately
         So that I receive clear feedback on any errors before the
         submission is processed

Acceptance Criteria:
         [Paste the complete Gherkin scenarios from your .feature file]
         [Do NOT summarize — the full Given/When/Then text goes here]

Tags:    concern:enrollment, bdd, sprint:14
```

**Critical rule — the acceptance criteria are the Gherkin scenarios, not a prose summary.** This is the core discipline. When the engineer reads the story, the acceptance criteria are directly executable. "Done" means every scenario passes — no interpretation required.
page_texts.29:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#step-8-size-the-story-correctly]

### Step 8: Size the Story Correctly

**The sizing guidelines:**

| Signal | Action |
|--------|--------|
| 3–15 scenarios, one concern, one `.feature` file | Right-sized — this is one story |
| More than 15 scenarios in one `.feature` file | Split the file into multiple files (e.g., `enrollment/submission.feature` and `enrollment/eligibility.feature`) — each becomes its own story |
| Fewer than 3 scenarios | Consider whether this is a standalone capability or part of a larger one — it may be a task within a bigger story, not a story itself |
| Multiple concern directories | Multiple stories — one story per concern |

**Story point guidance:**

Story points reflect implementation complexity, not specification complexity. As a product owner, you can provide a starting estimate based on scenario count:

| Scenario Count | Typical Range | Rationale |
|----------------|---------------|-----------|
| 3–5 scenarios | 2–3 points | Small, focused capability — one concern, few edge cases |
| 6–10 scenarios | 3–5 points | Medium capability — multiple paths, some complexity |
| 11–15 scenarios | 5–8 points | Large capability — significant business logic, many edge cases |

These are starting points for sprint planning. The engineer adjusts based on implementation complexity (which you cannot estimate — the scenarios describe _what_, not _how hard_).

**Output:** An Azure DevOps User Story with Gherkin acceptance criteria, properly tagged and estimated.

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#step-9-sprint-planning-and-handoff]

### Step 9: Sprint Planning and Handoff

When the User Story enters a sprint, two things happen:

1. **You brief the engineering team** on the scenarios — not reading them aloud, but explaining the business context: why this capability matters, what the business rules are, and which edge cases you care about most.

2. **The engineer creates GitHub Issues** from your story. You do not need to do this. The engineer uses [GUID-GOV-IMPL-003](../implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md) to create one GitHub Issue per `.feature` file per language (Python, C#, Java, Rust). Each Issue references the `@FR-` scenario IDs from your `.feature` file as its acceptance criteria.

**What you need to know about the decomposition:**

| Your Story | Engineer Creates | Why |
|------------|-----------------|-----|
| 1 story with 8 scenarios, 4 supported languages | 4 GitHub Issues (1 per language) | Each language is implemented independently — keeps each task small and reviewable |
| 1 story with 3 `.feature` files, 4 languages | 12 GitHub Issues (3 files × 4 languages) | Same principle — one file per language per issue |

You do not manage the GitHub Issues. You manage the ADO User Story. The engineer manages the issues.
page_texts.32:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#step-10-review-the-feature-file-before-commit]

### Step 10: Review the Feature File Before Commit

Before the `.feature` file is committed to the repository, the engineer sends it to you for final review. This is your last quality gate — after this, the scenarios become the executable test contract.

**Your review checklist:**

- [ ] The scenarios match the business requirement — nothing was lost in translation
- [ ] The concrete values are correct (amounts, codes, thresholds, dates)
- [ ] No scenarios were added that you did not author or approve
- [ ] No scenarios were removed or reworded
- [ ] The domain vocabulary matches the glossary
- [ ] You are comfortable that if every scenario passes, the capability is "done"

**If something is wrong:** Tell the engineer. The fix is a conversation, followed by an updated `.feature` file. The engineer does not unilaterally change your scenarios — they are your requirements.
page_texts.33:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#step-11-accept-the-implementation]

### Step 11: Accept the Implementation

Once the engineer's code is merged and the CI pipeline passes, your User Story is ready for acceptance.

**What has happened by this point:**

1. Your Gherkin scenarios are committed in the repository as `.feature` files
2. The engineer (or AI agent) has written code that makes every scenario pass
3. The CI pipeline has verified that every `@FR-` scenario passes in every supported language (Python, C#, Java, Rust)
4. A peer reviewer has approved the implementation PR

**What "done" means:**

The scenarios you wrote are passing as automated tests. The system does exactly what the scenarios say it does. There is no separate acceptance testing phase — the BDD suite _is_ the acceptance test. You already approved the specification (Step 10). The CI pipeline has verified the implementation matches it.

**Your actions:**

1. Verify the PR is merged and the CI pipeline is green (the engineer shows you this)
2. Close or update the ADO User Story
3. Move on to the next capability

**When to re-engage during implementation:**

| Situation | What Happens |
|-----------|-------------|
| Engineer finds a scenario is wrong | Engineer contacts you — you discuss and agree on the fix. A separate PR updates the `.feature` file. |
| Engineer discovers a missing edge case | Engineer contacts you — you decide whether to add it now or defer to a future sprint |
| CI passes but the demo looks wrong | Something outside the BDD scenarios is incorrect — the scenarios passed, but the UI, performance, or integration behavior was not covered. Add new scenarios for the gap. |

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-006-bdd-product-owner-playbook.md#common-questions]

## Common Questions

**Q: Do I need to learn Gherkin syntax?**
A: The basics take about 15 minutes: `Given` (setup), `When` (action), `Then` (expected result). AI handles the formatting. You focus on the business content. See the first section of [GUID-APP-IMPL-006](../../application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-006-bdd-gherkin-specification-authoring-guidance.md) for a complete reference.

**Q: What if I do not know all the edge cases?**
A: Start with what you know. AI will prompt you for common edge cases ("what happens if the input is null?", "what about concurrent access?"). You decide which are in scope. Missing edge cases can be added later as new scenarios — they do not invalidate existing ones.

**Q: Can the engineer change my scenarios?**
A: No. Scenarios are requirements. If an engineer discovers that a scenario is wrong or missing, they come back to you. The fix is a conversation, not a unilateral edit. See [GUID-GOV-PROC-010 — BDD Specification Change Management](GUID-GOV-PROC-010-bdd-specification-change-management-guidance.md) for the full loopback protocol, and the [BDD Lifecycle Strategy §7.0](../../../white-papers/engineering/bdd-lifecycle-strategy.md) on feature file immutability.

**Q: How do I know the AI-generated scenarios are correct?**
A: AI generates candidates based on your description. You validate them against your domain knowledge. AI is excellent at structure and edge case elicitation; it cannot know whether the business actually requires a specific behavior. Every scenario needs your sign-off.

**Q: What if our project only uses one language (e.g., just Python)?**
A: The process is the same — you just get fewer GitHub Issues downstream (1 per `.feature` file instead of 4). Your workflow does not change at all.

**Q: What is the `@FR-` tag and why do I care?**
A: It is a unique ID for each scenario (e.g., `@FR-ENR-SUB-010`). It lets engineers, CI pipelines, and traceability reports link your scenario to its implementation and test results. AI assigns them automatically using the project's naming convention. You only need to verify they are unique and correctly prefixed.

**Q: When should I NOT use BDD?**
A: BDD is for behavioral requirements — what the system does in response to inputs. It is not a good fit for non-functional requirements (performance targets, availability SLAs), infrastructure configuration, or UI layout specifications. Those remain prose requirements in ADO.
